genZNote: Needs actual lipids to grow in culture — skip the olive oil overlay and this organism just won't show up.

morphology.shape: Round to oval budding yeast with short septate hyphae

habitat.naturalHabitat: Human skin, especially sebum-rich areas (scalp, chest, back)
habitat.hostAssociation: Normal lipophilic skin commensal in virtually all adults; becomes pathogenic under certain conditions (humidity, sebum, immunosuppression)
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Requires exogenous lipids to grow — does not thrive outside a lipid-rich host environment

microscopy.stain: KOH wet mount of skin scrapings
microscopy.appearance: Classic 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance — short hyphal fragments (spaghetti) with clusters of round yeast cells (meatballs)

culture.media: Sabouraud dextrose agar overlaid with olive oil or other long-chain fatty acid source (lipid supplementation required)
culture.growthCharacteristics: Lipophilic — will not grow on standard Sabouraud agar without lipid supplementation
culture.colonyMorphology: Cream to yellowish, smooth to slightly wrinkled colonies

identificationClues: Classic 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance on KOH prep of skin scrapings (short hyphae plus round yeast clusters)
Lipophilic — requires lipid supplementation (e.g., olive oil overlay) to grow in culture; will not grow on plain Sabouraud agar
Causes hypo- or hyperpigmented, finely scaling patches on the trunk (tinea/pityriasis versicolor)
Can cause catheter-related fungemia in patients receiving lipid-based total parenteral nutrition

diseases: Tinea (pityriasis) versicolor — hypo/hyperpigmented scaly patches, typically on the trunk
Seborrheic dermatitis (associated, though causation is debated)
Catheter-associated fungemia, particularly in infants/patients on lipid-containing parenteral nutrition
virulenceFactors: Lipid dependence allowing colonization of sebaceous skin areas
Production of azelaic acid, which inhibits melanocyte tyrosinase and causes the characteristic pigmentary changes of tinea versicolor
clinicalImportance.transmission: Endogenous — part of normal skin flora; overgrowth triggered by heat, humidity, sebum production, or immunosuppression rather than person-to-person spread
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: Extremely common cause of tinea versicolor worldwide, especially in hot/humid climates and in young adults; catheter-related fungemia is a recognized complication in neonates/patients on lipid emulsion parenteral nutrition
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: Diagnosis of tinea versicolor is usually clinical plus KOH microscopy — culture is rarely needed and requires lipid-supplemented media if attempted

examFacts.shape: Round yeast with short septate hyphae
examFacts.keyBiochemicalReaction: Requires exogenous lipids to grow in culture
examFacts.importantTest: KOH prep showing 'spaghetti and meatballs' pattern
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: A lipid-dependent skin yeast producing the classic 'spaghetti and meatballs' microscopy pattern and hypo/hyperpigmented patches of tinea versicolor
